title: Rearranging Thermodynamic Formulas
source: Algebra & Maths Skills — Module 7 (the applied core)
summary:
This is the module that matters most: rearranging the **actual formulas** you meet in thermodynamics. The textbook almost never gives an equation in the form you need, so the skill of bending it to your target variable is the difference between getting stuck and getting the answer. The good news — under the surface it's the **same 7 patterns over and over**. Learn to recognise which one you're looking at, and every formula becomes routine.

The universal recipe never changes: **identify your target letter, list what's wrapped around it, undo those operations in reverse order, applying every step to both whole sides.** What changes is the *last wrapper* you have to peel — and that's what the 7 patterns name.

**Pattern 1 — isolate a factor (divide it out).** Your target is one factor in a product. Divide both sides by everything else. $Q = mc\Delta T \Rightarrow c = \dfrac{Q}{m\Delta T}$; $pV = mRT \Rightarrow T = \dfrac{pV}{mR}$. One move, works for the ideal-gas law, energy balances, exergy of a reservoir.

**Pattern 2 — variable in a denominator (lift it first).** If the target sits *underneath* a fraction, multiply both sides by it to bring it up, then isolate. $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q} \Rightarrow Q = \dfrac{W}{\eta}$; same for $COP = \dfrac{Q_L}{W}$ and $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$.

**Pattern 3 — a subtracted fraction (undo the '1−' first).** The classic trap: Carnot efficiency $\eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_L}{T_H}$. Move the constant across *before* touching the fraction: $\dfrac{T_L}{T_H} = 1-\eta$, then $T_L = T_H(1-\eta)$. The exergy factor $\left(1-\dfrac{T_0}{T}\right)$ and second-law efficiency work the same way.

**Pattern 4 — squared or under a root (do the root/square last).** Strip the factors, *then* apply the inverse. $KE = \tfrac12 mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2KE}{m}}$; a nozzle's $h_1 = h_2 + \dfrac{V_2^2}{2} \Rightarrow V_2 = \sqrt{2(h_1-h_2)}$.

**Pattern 5 — variable in an exponent (raise to the reciprocal power).** This is the one that stops people cold in Chapter 7. The isentropic relation $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k}$ hides $P_2$ inside a fractional power. To free it, **raise both sides to the reciprocal exponent** $\dfrac{k}{k-1}$: $P_2 = P_1\left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{k/(k-1)}$. A power is undone by the reciprocal power, just as a square is undone by a square root.

**Pattern 6 — a mixture / table relation (solve for quality).** Every saturated-mixture property has the form $y = y_f + x\,y_{fg}$ (for $y = v, u, h, s$). Make the quality the subject: $x = \dfrac{y - y_f}{y_{fg}}$ — subtract $y_f$, divide by $y_{fg}$.

**Pattern 7 — variable inside a log (undo with exp), or collect terms.** When the unknown is trapped in a logarithm — the entropy relation $\Delta s = c_p\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$ (const $P$) — **exponentiate both sides**: $T_2 = T_1\,e^{\Delta s/c_p}$. Logs and exponentials are inverses, exactly like square/root. And for an energy or entropy balance ($Q - W = \Delta U$), you just collect and move terms across the '='.

Carry away the reflex: **name the pattern, then apply its inverse last.** Rearrange symbolically *before* plugging numbers — you get a reusable formula and a clean check. And in every efficiency, gas-law, entropy or exergy formula, temperatures are **absolute (kelvin)**.

equations.name: Pattern 1 — isolate a factor (divide it out)
equations.useWhen: Your target is one factor in a product. Divide both sides by everything else that multiplies it — one move.
equations.note: Same pattern for $pV = mRT$, boundary work $W_b = P\,\Delta V$, and exergy of heat $X = T_0 S_{gen}$.

equations.name: Pattern 2 — variable in a denominator (lift it first)
equations.useWhen: The target sits underneath a fraction. Multiply both sides by it to bring it to the top, then isolate as usual.
equations.note: Don't try to divide it out while it's in the denominator — lift it up with multiplication first.

equations.name: Pattern 3 — a subtracted fraction (undo the '1−' first)
equations.useWhen: The unknown is buried in a fraction that is being subtracted (Carnot efficiency, the exergy factor $1-T_0/T$, second-law efficiency). Move the constant across the '=' first, then clear the fraction.
equations.note: Peeling the +/− before the ×/÷ is reverse-BIDMAS. Temperatures absolute (K).

equations.name: Pattern 4 — squared or under a root (root/square last)
equations.useWhen: The target is squared (take the root last) or under a root (square last). Strip away the surrounding ×/÷ first, then apply the inverse to the *whole* other side.
equations.note: Square and square-root are inverses. Keep the positive root for a physical quantity (speed, radius).

equations.name: Pattern 5 — variable in an exponent (raise to the reciprocal power)
rearrangements: \text{raise both sides to the reciprocal power } \tfrac{k}{k-1}
equations.useWhen: The unknown is trapped inside a fractional power — the isentropic ideal-gas relations of Chapter 7. Raise both sides to the reciprocal exponent to free it.
equations.note: $\tfrac{k}{k-1}$ is the reciprocal of $\tfrac{k-1}{k}$; raising to it cancels the power, just as a square root cancels a square. The single trickiest rearrangement in the thermo course.

equations.name: Pattern 6 — mixture / table relation (solve for quality)
equations.useWhen: Finding the quality $x$ of a saturated liquid–vapour mixture from any of its properties. Subtract the saturated-liquid value $y_f$, then divide by $y_{fg}$.
equations.note: The same relation gives $x$ from $v$, $u$, $h$ or $s$ — whichever the tables and problem hand you.

equations.name: Pattern 7 — variable in a log (undo with exp), or collect terms
rearrangements: Q - W = \Delta U \;\Rightarrow\; W = Q - \Delta U
equations.useWhen: The unknown is inside a logarithm — exponentiate both sides to free it. Or, in an energy/entropy balance, simply collect and move terms across the '='.
equations.note: $\ln$ and $e^{(\cdot)}$ are inverses (see [[al04]]). For balances, moving a term across the '=' flips its sign.

glossary.definition: Isolate a factor · lift a denominator · undo a subtracted fraction · root/square last · reciprocal power for an exponent · quality from a mixture relation · exp to undo a log (and collect terms in balances). Name the pattern, apply its inverse last.
Rearrange until your target variable stands alone on one side, $\text{target} = (\text{everything else})$. The core skill this module drills.
$P = P_{atm} + \rho g h$. To find depth, isolate $h$: $h = (P - P_{atm})/(\rho g)$ — a Pattern-1 isolate-a-factor after moving $P_{atm}$.
$pV = mRT$. Divide by the product of the others to get any single variable (Pattern 1). $R$ is the specific gas constant.
$\eta = W/Q$; a fraction, so the heat in $Q = W/\eta$ comes from lifting the denominator (Pattern 2).
Heat moved ÷ work in for a fridge/heat pump. Carnot heat pump $COP = T_H/(T_H - T_L)$ — a denominator and a difference to rearrange.
$T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)^{(k-1)/k}$. Solving for $P_2$ needs the reciprocal power $k/(k-1)$ (Pattern 5) — the trickiest thermo rearrangement.
Vapour mass fraction of a saturated mixture, from $y = y_f + x\,y_{fg}$ ⇒ $x = (y - y_f)/y_{fg}$ (Pattern 6). Works for $v, u, h, s$.
For an adiabatic nozzle $h_1 = h_2 + V_2^2/2$; the exit speed $V_2 = \sqrt{2(h_1 - h_2)}$ is a Pattern-4 root.
$\dot m = AV/v$ (area × velocity ÷ specific volume). Rearranges to $V = \dot m v/A$ — Pattern 1/2.
$\Delta s = c_p\ln(T_2/T_1) - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$. At constant $P$, freeing $T_2$ needs the exponential (Pattern 7): $T_2 = T_1 e^{\Delta s/c_p}$.
$X_{dest} = T_0\,S_{gen}$; the entropy generation $S_{gen} = X_{dest}/T_0$ is a one-step isolate (Pattern 1).
Kelvin. Efficiency, gas-law, entropy and exergy formulas all require it — converting °C wrong is a top source of rearrangement errors.

tips: **Name the pattern first.** Before touching the algebra, ask which of the 7 you're looking at — that tells you the *last* inverse to apply (divide, lift, move the 1−, root, reciprocal power, mixture, or exp).
**Exponent ⇒ reciprocal power.** To free a variable inside $(\cdot)^{(k-1)/k}$, raise both sides to $k/(k-1)$. This is the Chapter-7 isentropic move and the one worth drilling until automatic.
**Log ⇒ exponential.** If the unknown is inside $\ln(\cdot)$, apply $e^{(\cdot)}$ to both sides. $\Delta s = c_p\ln(T_2/T_1) \Rightarrow T_2 = T_1 e^{\Delta s/c_p}$.
**Subtracted fraction: kill the constant first.** For $\eta = 1 - T_L/T_H$, move the 1 across *before* clearing the fraction. Reaching for the fraction first is the classic mistake.
**Denominator: lift, don't divide.** If your target is underneath, multiply both sides by it first, then isolate. Never try to divide it away while it's still in the denominator.
**Rearrange symbolically, then substitute.** Get the formula into $\text{target} = \ldots$ before any numbers — reusable, fewer rounding errors, and easy to sanity-check.
**Kelvin, always.** Any formula with efficiency, the gas law, entropy or exergy needs absolute temperature — convert °C → K before you rearrange or substitute.
